title: ‘Agnostic’ mayor supports mixed energy supplies
full_text:
The mayor whose regional council is considering a proposal for Australia’s largest data centre says a mix of energy sources is key to attracting investment in the burgeoning $150bn industry.
Speaking to The Australian after a Singapore-based developer lodged plans to build a data centre on a 725-hectare plot of land northwest of Brisbane, Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith said the region’s proximity to gas and coal-fired power stations and the growing renewables industry meant it was well placed to cash in on the AI data centre boom.
“We very close to an extensive amount of infrastructure already when it comes to energy in the Western Downs,” he said. “In that Braemar area, we have gas-fired power stations. It’s not a long way from a coal-fired power station. We have a building renewable industry … wind, solar and large-scale battery.” Western Downs regional council encompasses Dalby, an area 250km northwest of Brisbane. But as states look to attract data centre investment, a fiery showdown has erupted between the federal government and some states after Energy Minister Chris Bowen decreed data centres be fuelled entirely by renewable power.
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has put forward his own data centre framework as he defied the commonwealth’s renewable-only energy mandate for data centres. He has said his planning framework was designed to show the industry that Queensland was “open for business and a place to invest again”, while listening to community voices.
“This is about data sovereignty for our country, it’s about respecting communities’ wishes and resources, and it’s about creating the jobs of tomorrow while protecting the Queensland of today,” he said. Asked if he sided with the Queensland government in resisting the commonwealth’s push for next-generation data centres to use renewable energy with gas firming, Mr Smith said he was “energy agnostic … if it’s gas or wind we’re neither here nor there.”
